newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr uptrend dog-eared after mauling.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr uptrend dog-eared after mauling.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept a low profile through a holiday-hit session Monday after an offshore slide sundered support and soured sentiment on the currency.

Dealers said U.S. investment banks decided to dump the dollar late Friday following a week of fruitless attempts at US$0.8020 resistance. The selling overwhelmed US$0.7950 chart support and saw it down over 3/4 cent at one stage to US$0.7888.

Exporter and Japanese demand prompted a modest bounce today but soon foundered in the face of offers at US$0.7920, leaving traders wondering if the dollar's five week long, three cent wide bull run had finally met its matador.
By 4.40 pm (0640 GMT) a dog-eared dollar was lying at US$0.7915/20 after folding from US$0.7962/67 late here Friday and a US$0.8020 peak just a week ago.

Analysts pencilled support in at US$0.7885 and US$0.7860, with the pivotal chart level being US$0.7810. Resistance was lined up at US$0.7930 and US$0.7950 and many felt the currency would have to recover 80 cents to restore confidence in the longer term uptrend.
It's performance was much more mixed on the crosses where a firm U.S. dollar lent support against the yen, but U.S. funds had been busy switching into Canadian and New Zealand dollars.
That saw the local currency slip only slightly to 87.50/60 yen from 87.63/73 late here Friday, but slide to C$1.0843/54 from C$1.0922/33 and NZ$1.1359/75 from NZ$1.1444/62.

There was also much talk Japanese investors were thinking of switching from A$ denominated samurai bonds in search of better yields or reduced currency risk. Kiwi dollar samurais had been in demand for weeks, but dealers said the market was small and illiquid and a far bigger risk was posed by US$ issues.
The chief attraction of Australian over U.S. bonds were their yield premium, but this had narrowed sharply following the 0.5 point cut in domestic interest rates on July 31.
Many analysts here also expected another cut before year end taking rates to 6.50 percent, while U.S. rates were seen rising by between 0.25 and 0.50 point from the present 5.25 percent.

The gap was even thinner when it came to bonds, where the yield premium offered by an Australian two year issue -- a time frame favoured in dual currency samurais -- was already down to a svelte 71 basis points and could even approach parity if official rates in the two countries moved as feared.
"In such a scenario it would be hard to see why Japanese investors would still favour A$ samurais over US$ issues with their advantages of lower risk and greater liquidity," said one.

Analysts emphasised this scenario was speculative -- the soft U.S. inflation and sales data Friday had already made a Fed hike look less likely this month -- but the risk was real and would argue against a sustained rise above 80 cents until 1997.

Another major plank in the bullish case has been expectations that a synchronised upswing in world growth would drive commodity prices higher -- important as commodities make up over 60 percent of Australia's exports.
Some of the necessary requirements had fallen into place -- U.S. growth was running at a robust pace while both Germany and Japan were showing genuine signs of recovery.
However, this economic upturn had yet to produce the sort of acceleration in inflation which had typically heralded a sustained appreciation in commodity prices in the past.
Most analysts did still feel world growth would recover enough to lift the demand for, and price of, commodities, but probably not until well into 1997.
That in turn left the Australian dollar looking rather over extended on a three month view, they said.
In trade weighted terms the currency fell to 58.4 from 58.7 late here Friday.
